newsitem.title: UK: N.Europe sugar beet crop seen down after adverse weather.
newsitem.headline: N.Europe sugar beet crop seen down after adverse weather.

text.p: Production prospects for northern European beet growers, the mainstay of the European Union's (EU) 1996/97 sugar crop, are still mixed as recent rainfall balanced the effects of an earlier drought and adverse spring weather.
Analysts said cold dry conditions after drilling, followed by dry weather in July and August, have hampered beet development although many areas have since received rain.
Estimates for this year's crop showed a marginal decline against 1995/96 with trade house Czarnikow pegging output at 16.8 million tonnes raw value versus a previous 17.02 million.
France, the EU's largest beet grower, should produce less sugar this year as results of the fourth and last beet field test showed that the crop had made only a partial recovery.
The French sugar intervention board FIRS said on Monday it was maintaining its 1996/97 estimate of 3.9 million tonnes, after last year's output of 4.2 million tonnes.
Analysts said insufficient moisture between the third and fourth tests had limited the crop's progress.
In Germany, the fourth test result published on Monday showed implied sugar yields had progressed over the last two weeks and should support a better final crop figure.
"It doesn't look unfavourable any more, sugar production could now exceed earlier forecasts if we get the right mixture of rainfall and sunshine during the beet campaign," said one.
Leading sugar association WVZ is maintaining its output forecast at 3.87 million tonnes, up 1.9 percent.
In the latest test, sugar contents and beet weights were both higher than last year, with good plant densities also pointing to higher sugar yields.
In Britain, the recent rains over beet growing areas have helped reverse the effects of the earlier dry weather and the initial gloomy prognosis for this year's crop.
Amounts of sugar per root and root weights were now above 1995 levels, although sugar contents were still lagging behind.
British Sugar has said the crop has made good progress and was on course for an average result.
Sugar production in another of the region's leading growers, the Netherlands, was also expected to be slightly lower this year due to the dry weather, although the rains have helped.
Belgium and other Benelux countries are only about one per cent down on last year according to their beet test results despite early drought and late rain.
